lessons.title: Shortest path, no media proxy
lessons.why: Teams media hates hairpins and proxies. Bandwidth is the expensive way to hide a bad path.
depends: A picture of the real egress
body: Microsoft’s QoS and network articles tell you to keep the path short: on the order of three to five hops from the client to your edge, and a short path from the ISP to Microsoft. Proxies in the media path are a known way to damage calls. ExpressRoute is not required.
Draw the path a branch actually uses. If that branch backhauls across a continent to egress, you already know why RTT is high. A fatter pipe will not shorten the fiber.

chart.title: Hop budget
chart.note: Planning guidance from the QoS article, not a measurement of your network.

lessons.say: Local egress, no media proxy, ExpressRoute not required.
lessons.fault: A branch hairpins through headquarters and every call shows long RTT.
lessons.listen: Keep Teams media on a short path to the internet. Do not send it through a proxy or a distant hairpin.

lessons.title: The port and DSCP table
lessons.why: This table is the QoS interview. It is also the ACL.
body: The QoS article’s initial ranges are audio UDP or TCP 50000–50019 at DSCP 46 EF, video 50020–50039 at 34 AF41, sharing 50040–50059 at 18 AF21, and calling and meeting signaling 50070–50089 at 40 CS5. Signaling ports are not configurable.
Browser joins do not use those fixed ranges. Mac and mobile hard-code audio as EF. Windows can follow policy, and the client process to match is ms-teams.exe, not the previous client’s name.

chart.note: Bar length is the DSCP value from the QoS article.

lessons.say: Audio is 46 on ports 50000 to 50019. I can place the other three without a card.
lessons.fault: An ACL matches the old client or the wrong port range, so marks never land.
lessons.listen: Audio DSCP 46, video 34, sharing 18, signaling 40. Browser joins do not use the fixed client ports.

lessons.title: VPN and the split tunnel
lessons.why: A full-tunnel VPN adds delay and hides the office subnet from emergency location and from CQD.
body: Microsoft recommends that you avoid real-time media on a VPN. QoS inside the tunnel only prioritizes traffic inside a path that is already longer. Split tunnel is the usual way to let media go direct while other traffic stays on the VPN.
A VPN pool labeled as headquarters will make CQD accuse the wrong building and can make dynamic emergency calling report the wrong place. Treat the VPN range as its own site, or as not a site.
lessons.say: I keep real-time media off the full-tunnel VPN, and I do not label the VPN pool as HQ.
lessons.fault: Remote users show high jitter and DSCP 0, and CQD draws them inside headquarters.
lessons.listen: Do not send Teams media through a full-tunnel VPN. Do not call the VPN pool a building.

lessons.title: Bandwidth you can calculate
lessons.why: 64 kbit/s is the payload. The link carries headers too.
body: G.711 at 20 milliseconds is 160 bytes of payload. Add 40 bytes of IP, UDP, and RTP and the call is 80 kbit/s per direction at layer 3. Add an 18-byte Ethernet header and it is 87.2 kbit/s. G.729 at the same interval is 20 bytes of payload, 24 kbit/s at layer 3.

Silence suppression and a different packet interval change the average. Size the busy hour at the packetization you actually configure, in both directions, for the concurrent calls you actually expect. A yearly average divided by eight is not a busy hour.

lessons.title: Proving the mark survived
lessons.why: A client policy that the WAN undoes is not QoS.
body: Capture at the network egress, not only on the PC. You want the DSCP value on the wire after the VPN, the switch, and the router. Port mirroring is the usual way.
If audio ports 50000–50019 leave the building marked 0, the client policy missed or a device rewrote the mark. Fix that before you argue about codecs.
lessons.say: I capture at the egress and show DSCP 46 still on the audio ports.
lessons.fault: The laptop looks correct and the WAN sees best effort.
lessons.listen: Prove QoS at the network egress. A mark that dies on the VPN is not a design.

lessons.title: ExpressRoute is not the requirement
lessons.why: A private circuit is a purchasing choice. It is not the Teams network requirement.
body: Teams is designed to work over the internet with local egress. If your organization also has ExpressRoute, follow the current network documentation for which traffic belongs there. Do not assume media is automatically better on the private path.
QoS still has to be consistent on whatever path you chose. A private path with no marks and extra distance is a slower best-effort network.

chart.title: Decision, not a default
chart.note: Both can be valid. The article does not require ExpressRoute.

lessons.say: Teams does not require ExpressRoute. Local internet egress is the normal plan.
lessons.fault: Media is forced onto a long private path and delay gets worse.
lessons.listen: Do not buy ExpressRoute to make Teams legal. Design the path, then mark it.
